{{Short description|Sum of the static and dynamic pressure}}
{{More citations needed|date=April 2009}}
In [[fluid dynamics]], '''stagnation pressure''', also
referred to as '''total pressure''', is what the pressure would be if all the kinetic energy of the fluid were to be converted into pressure in a reversible manner.;<ref name=Clancy/>{{rp|§ 3.2}} it is defined as the sum of the free-stream [[static pressure]] and the free-stream [[dynamic pressure]].<ref>[https://scienceworld.wolfram.com/physics/StagnationPressure.html Stagnation Pressure] at Eric Weisstein's World of Physics (Wolfram Research)</ref>

The Bernoulli equation applicable to [[incompressible flow]] shows that the stagnation pressure is equal to the dynamic pressure and static pressure combined.<ref name=Clancy>Clancy, L.J. (1975), ''Aerodynamics'', Pitman Publishing Limited, London. {{ISBN|0-273-01120-0}}</ref>{{rp|§ 3.5}}   In [[compressible flow]]s, stagnation pressure is also equal to total pressure as well, provided that the fluid entering the stagnation point is brought to rest [[Isentropic flow|isentropically]].<ref name=Clancy/>{{rp|§ 3.12}}

Stagnation pressure is sometimes referred to as [[pitot pressure]] because the two pressures are equal.

==Magnitude==
The magnitude of stagnation pressure can be derived from [[Bernoulli's principle|Bernoulli equation]]<ref>[http://www.engineeringtoolbox.com/bernouilli-equation-d_183.html Equation 4], Bernoulli Equation - The Engineering Toolbox</ref><ref name=Clancy/>{{rp|§ 3.5}} for [[incompressible flow]] and no height changes. For any two points 1 and 2:

:<math>P_1 + \tfrac{1}{2} \rho v_1^2 = P_2 + \tfrac{1}{2} \rho v_2^2</math>

The two points of interest are 1) in the freestream flow at relative speed <math>v</math> where the pressure is called the "static" pressure, (for example well away from an airplane moving at speed <math>v</math>); and 2) at a "stagnation" point where the fluid is at rest with respect to the measuring apparatus (for example at the end of a pitot tube in an airplane).

Then 
:<math>P_\text{static} + \tfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2 = P_\text{stagnation} + \tfrac{1}{2} \rho (0)^2</math>

or<ref>Houghton, E.L and Carpenter P.W. ''Aerodynamics'' (2003), Section 2.3.1</ref>

:<math>P_\text{stagnation}=P_\text{static} + \tfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2  </math>

where:
:<math>P_\text{stagnation}</math> is the stagnation pressure
:<math>\rho\;</math> is the fluid density
:<math>v</math> is the speed of fluid
:<math>P_\text{static}</math> is the static pressure

So the stagnation pressure is increased over the static pressure, by the amount <math>\tfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2</math> which is called the "dynamic" or "ram" pressure because it results from fluid motion.  In our airplane example, the stagnation pressure would be atmospheric pressure plus the dynamic pressure.

In [[compressible flow]] however, the fluid density is higher at the stagnation point than at the static point. Therefore, <math>\tfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2</math> can't be used for the dynamic pressure. For many purposes in compressible flow, the stagnation [[enthalpy]] or [[stagnation temperature]] plays a role similar to the stagnation pressure in incompressible flow.<ref>Clancy, L.J. ''Aerodynamics'', Section 3.12</ref>

==Compressible flow==
Stagnation pressure is the static pressure a gas retains when brought to rest [[isentropic process|isentropical]]ly from [[Mach number]] ''M''.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20210324235239/https://www.grc.nasa.gov/WWW/BGH/Images/naca1135.pdf Equations 35,44], Equations, Tables and Charts for Compressible Flow</ref>

:<math>\frac{p_t}{p} = \left(1 + \frac{\gamma -1}{2} M^2\right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}}\, </math>

or, assuming an [[isentropic]] process, the stagnation pressure can be calculated from the ratio of stagnation temperature to static temperature:

:<math>\frac{p_t}{p} = \left(\frac{T_t}{T}\right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}}\,</math>

where:

:<math>p_t</math> is the stagnation pressure
:<math>p</math> is the static pressure
:<math>T_t</math> is the stagnation temperature
:<math>T</math> is the static temperature
:<math>\gamma</math> is the [[Heat capacity ratio|ratio of specific heats]]

The above derivation holds only for the case when the gas is assumed to be [[Perfect gas|calorically perfect]] (specific heats and the ratio of the specific heats <math>\gamma</math> are assumed to be constant with temperature).
